$comment: EFB-71 boundary discipline, query-string half. Routes that read query params WITHOUT parseRouteQuery (see docs/BOUNDARY_DISCIPLINE.md). Same ratchet contract as scripts/boundary-allowlist.json: it may only shrink, every entry carries a sunset, scripts/check-boundary-query.mjs FAILS once that date passes rather than warning, and sunsets more than 180 days out are rejected outright. New routes may not be added here - write them against parseRouteQuery.
$reAudit: EFB-87. Every entry here is re-audited against detection on every run, and a mismatch FAILS - same rule and same reasoning as scripts/boundary-allowlist.json, where the long form lives. An entry whose route now reads through parseRouteQuery, or in which no query-read marker appears at all, or which names no route the scan can see, has stopped describing anything. The escape is an entry-level "scanner_blind_reason" saying in writing why detection cannot see a read that is really there; an empty one is rejected. Note this is NOT the mass-declaration pattern rejected below: it applies only to entries that already exist, one sentence at a time, which is precisely the narrowness the $declarationDebt objection turns on.
$declarationDebt: There is NO noQuery list here, and that is a deliberate, dated gap rather than a claim of safety. The body check requires a human declaration for every route where no read was detected, because reads hide behind helpers the scanner cannot follow. Applied here that would have meant ~50 declarations written in a single commit - query params ride every verb, not just the body-bearing three - and fifty entries added in one sitting is not fifty routes read. It is a checkbox, and it is worse than honest silence because it launders an inference into a human declaration that would be cited later as verification. A declaration's evidentiary weight cannot exceed what the process that produced it could have earned. So the check instead PRINTS its blind spot on every successful run ('N handlers had no detected query read - that is not proof they read none'), and the noQuery declarations land in the per-subsystem migration tickets below, where someone is actually reading the route. Follow-up: the per-subsystem query-migration ticket filed after EFB-71, which is where each noQuery declaration gets made by someone reading that route. Deliberately not pre-assigned a number here - a number written before the ticket exists is a pointer that may resolve to something else entirely, which is how EFB-71 itself nearly shipped pointing at EFB-69.
